{"additions":375,"autoMergeRequest":null,"baseRefName":"main","body":"Part 3 of #2190's [agreed split](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2190#issuecomment-5499945525), following the merged canonical resolver in #2241 and checkpoint migration in #2254.

Session construction, adoption, and sweep still use separate paths to resolve Git metadata. This PR moves the explicit-root consumers to `gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata`, so the canonical resolver supplies the common directory and worktree ID while each caller keeps its own storage and failure policy.

## Session-store construction

Previously, constructing a session store for a known worktree root ran `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, even though the root was already known.

`NewStateStoreForWorktree` now resolves `WorktreeMetadata.CommonDir` directly. Known-root construction therefore starts no Git subprocesses and checks the current metadata on every call. For example, if `commondir` is changed to point at a missing directory after a successful construction, the next construction fails. Repairing the metadata makes construction succeed again and preserves access to the saved session. Inherited `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_COMMON_DIR`, and `GIT_WORK_TREE` values also cannot redirect an explicitly scoped store into another repository.

`NewStateStore`, the CWD constructor, intentionally stays on `gitdir.CommonDir`. The strategy's per-session state lock resolves through that same function, and the store and its lock must agree on one common directory. If the store moved to the canonical resolver alone, an exported `GIT_DIR` would place state files in the worktree's own `.git` while the lock went to the repository `GIT_DIR` names. Two writers of one state file would then hold different locks. Keeping both on one resolver also keeps split `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` setups working for session state. The CWD store moves to the canonical resolver together with the lock.

The common directory still feeds the existing rooted store. Linked worktrees share session files, and empty-root rejection, test isolation, no-follow I/O, atomic writes, and locking remain in place.

## Adoption and sweep

Adoption uses the canonical resolver for source and target worktree IDs. This removes its dependency on the legacy parser's expected directory names. A linked worktree backed by a bare repository named `storage`, for example, can now resolve its ID from `storage/worktrees/<id>`.

Hook paths still derive worktree IDs with `paths.GetWorktreeID`. Both resolvers yield the same ID for main and linked worktrees under `.git/` or `.bare/`. Only the canonical resolver also accepts a bare repository with any other name, and hooks cannot start sessions in that layout yet. Hook callers move to the canonical resolver with the strategy migration.

The source and target retain different failure policies. If source metadata cannot resolve, adoption can still match the session by its recorded worktree path. If target metadata cannot resolve, adoption stops before saving the adopted state. The combined Git query in `stateStoreForWorktree` stays because it validates an arbitrary user-supplied repository; a directory that merely contains an empty `.git` folder must still be rejected. Source-retirement rollback remains unchanged.

Sweep now resolves metadata from the worktree root it has already discovered. If that fails, it skips spawning. On success, it uses the common directory for the existing repository-wide throttle, so session starts in different worktrees continue to share the same throttle marker.

## Why the legacy APIs and cache remain

`session.GetGitCommonDir`, the cache-clearing API, and `gitdir`'s common-directory resolver and cache still serve the CWD session store, the session lock, strategy, and other consumers outside this slice. Removing them now would require migrating those callers too. Their deletion waits until those callers have migrated and been verified.

This PR changes three production files and their tests, plus a comment-only fix in `gitdir/gitdir.go` that drops a stale list of callers. The ownership guard remains active, and its ledger reasons now name the callers that still use the legacy resolvers. Rooted-handle lifetime and the strategy and session-lock migration stay with their existing owners.

## Verification

- `mise run lint`: passed with zero issues after merging main.
- `mise run test:integration`: passed.
- `mise run test`: passed except for two tests that timed out while a second copy of the suite was running on the same machine. They were `TestExtractPluginBinary_OversizeEntryIsRejected`, which hit the package's 10-minute limit, and `TestInstallHooks_ReclaimedChainRunsEachHookOnce/bash_template`, whose hook was killed. Both pass on their own with `-race`, and neither touches session state or locking.
- After merging main: session, gitrepo, strategy session-state, hook, and preview tests, plus adoption, sweep, and pending-checkpoint tests, pass. The pending-preview tests pass now that #2770 is in.

Focused tests cover linked-worktree save/load/clear, invalid roots, explicit-root metadata damage and repair, inherited Git variables on explicit roots, and adoption validation and source-path fallback. They also cover bare-backed worktree IDs and sweep failure/throttle behavior. `TestSessionStateAndLockHonorExportedGitDir` pins that the CWD store and its lock land in the same common directory when `GIT_DIR` points at another repository and in a split `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` layout. It failed against the earlier revision of this branch and passes now. Existing tests exercise rooted storage, symlink refusal, and adoption rollback.

Real Git Trace2 events show constructor subprocess counts:

| Construction path | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CWD | 1 common-directory query | 1 common-directory query (unchanged) |
| Explicit root | 1 | 0 |

The Trace2 test includes a positive control that launches Git and checks that an additional event is recorded. These measurements cover store construction, not total hook latency.

**The regression:** [session_sweep.go:241](cmd/entire/cli/session_sweep.go:241)

Session construction and adoption still use separate paths to resolve Git metadata. This PR moves the explicit-root consumers to `gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata`, so the canonical resolver supplies the common directory and worktree ID while each caller keeps its own storage and failure policy.

## Session-store construction

Previously, constructing a session store for a known worktree root ran `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, even though the root was already known.

`NewStateStoreForWorktree` now resolves `WorktreeMetadata.CommonDir` directly. Known-root construction therefore starts no Git subprocesses and checks the current metadata on every call. For example, if `commondir` is changed to point at a missing directory after a successful construction, the next construction fails. Repairing the metadata makes construction succeed again and preserves access to the saved session. Inherited `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_COMMON_DIR`, and `GIT_WORK_TREE` values also cannot redirect an explicitly scoped store into another repository.

`NewStateStore`, the CWD constructor, intentionally stays on `gitdir.CommonDir`. The strategy's per-session state lock resolves through that same function, and the store and its lock must agree on one common directory. If the store moved to the canonical resolver alone, an exported `GIT_DIR` would place state files in the worktree's own `.git` while the lock went to the repository `GIT_DIR` names. Two writers of one state file would then hold different locks. Keeping both on one resolver also keeps split `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` setups working for session state. The CWD store moves to the canonical resolver together with the lock.

The common directory still feeds the existing rooted store. Linked worktrees share session files, and empty-root rejection, test isolation, no-follow I/O, atomic writes, and locking remain in place.

## Adoption

Adoption uses the canonical resolver for source and target worktree IDs. This removes its dependency on the legacy parser's expected directory names. A linked worktree backed by a bare repository named `storage`, for example, can now resolve its ID from `storage/worktrees/<id>`.

Hook paths still derive worktree IDs with `paths.GetWorktreeID`. Both resolvers yield the same ID for main and linked worktrees under `.git/` or `.bare/`. Only the canonical resolver also accepts a bare repository with any other name, and hooks cannot start sessions in that layout yet. Hook callers move to the canonical resolver with the strategy migration.

The source and target retain different failure policies. If source metadata cannot resolve, adoption can still match the session by its recorded worktree path. If target metadata cannot resolve, adoption stops before saving the adopted state. The combined Git query in `stateStoreForWorktree` stays because it validates an arbitrary user-supplied repository; a directory that merely contains an empty `.git` folder must still be rejected. Source-retirement rollback remains unchanged.

## Why the legacy APIs and cache remain

`session.GetGitCommonDir`, the cache-clearing API, and `gitdir`'s common-directory resolver and cache still serve the CWD session store, the session lock, the session sweep, strategy, and other consumers outside this slice. Removing them now would require migrating those callers too. Their deletion waits until those callers have migrated and been verified.

The sweep stays on `session.GetGitCommonDir` on purpose. It finds stuck sessions through the CWD store, so its throttle marker has to come from the same resolver. Moving the sweep alone to the canonical resolver would break split `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` layouts: the work tree has no `.git`, so the sweep would find stuck sessions and then skip spawning on every session start. The sweep moves together with the CWD store.

This PR changes two production files and their tests, plus a comment-only fix in `gitdir/gitdir.go` that drops a stale list of callers. The ownership guard remains active, and its ledger reasons now name the callers that still use the legacy resolvers. Rooted-handle lifetime and the strategy and session-lock migration stay with their existing owners.

- `mise run check`: passed after keeping the sweep on its existing resolver, including formatting, zero-issue lint, unit and integration tests, and the deterministic Vogon and roger-roger canaries.

They also cover bare-backed worktree IDs. `TestSessionStateAndLockHonorExportedGitDir` pins that the CWD store and its lock land in the same common directory when `GIT_DIR` points at another repository and in a split `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` layout. It failed against the earlier revision of this branch and passes now. Existing tests exercise rooted storage, symlink refusal, and adoption rollback.

Real Git Trace2 events show constructor subprocess counts:

| Construction path | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CWD | 1 common-directory query | 1 common-directory query (unchanged) |
| Explicit root | 1 | 0 |

The Trace2 test includes a positive control that launches Git and checks that an additional event is recorded. These measurements cover store construction, not total hook latency.

2. The source store and the source worktree ID can come from different repos (cmd/entire/cli/session_adopt.go:576). stateStoreForWorktree runs git -C <wt> rev-parse, which honors GIT_DIR. bestEffortAdoptWorktreeID reads the .git file on disk and ignores the environment..

Here's where the review stands. Findings 1, 2, 5 and 8 are caused by this PR. Findings 3, 6 and 7 were already on `main`, and 4 is an old pattern this PR moved into a new helper. Nothing is edited yet; you'll find the fix I propose, and an alternative, below.

**What I checked**

| # | Verdict | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Import state goes missing or to the wrong repo | **Real regression** | Import's only call is `NewStateStoreForWorktree(ctx, repoRoot)`, and `repoRoot` comes from `paths.WorktreeRoot`, which honors `GIT_DIR`. Checkpoints go through `openRepository`, which honors it too. Before this PR, `gitdir.CommonDirForWorktree` ran git with the environment inherited, so all three agreed. In a split layout the new resolver fails (I confirmed this earlier in a scratch repo) and the store ends up in a different repo from the checkpoints. |
| 2. Adoption accepts worktrees the hooks reject | **Real, but "stuck" is overstated** | Hooks call `paths.GetWorktreeID` only when a session has no saved state yet (`initializeSession`), plus once on a best-effort path that ignores errors. An adopted session already has state, so its turns don't hit that call. But new sessions in those layouts still fail, so adoption accepts layouts that session start rejects. #2305 already moves both of those hook calls. |
| 3. Source store and source ID come from different repos | **Real, but already on `main`** | The source ID used to come from `paths.GetWorktreeID`, which also reads `.git` from disk and ignores `GIT_DIR`. This PR swaps one env-blind resolver for another, so the disagreement isn't new. |
| 4. Silent fallback | Old pattern (`main` dropped the error the same way), easy fix | This PR moved it into one helper, so a Debug log is one line. |
| 5. Unused `ctx` | Real | Goes away if the store goes back to the git subprocess. |
| 6. Root path printed twice in the error | Already on `main` | Both layers add the root to the error. One-line fix. |
| 7. Source ID looked up twice | Already on `main` | `main` also looks it up more than once. Small fix. |
| 8. `filepath.Abs` dropped | Real | Goes away if the store is reverted. |

**Root cause:** the on-disk resolver ignores `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE`. In this PR, most of the roots treated as "explicit" are actually found from the CWD through `paths.WorktreeRoot`, which honors those variables. Only adoption's source path is really supplied by the user. That's the same mistake as the sweep, and the third time a pair that has to agree got split: store and lock, the sweep's list and throttle, and now adoption and hooks.

**Option A: fix it in this PR (recommended)**
- **Store (1, 5, 8):** point `NewStateStoreForWorktree` back at `gitdir.CommonDirForWorktree`, which restores `main`'s behavior. The cost is losing the "explicit root starts 0 git subprocesses" win, and an exported `GIT_DIR` takes priority over the explicit root again. The test-isolation guard still fails loudly if that points outside the temp directory.
- **Hooks (2):** move `initializeSession` and `reconcileWorktreePathForResumedTurn` to `ResolveWorktreeMetadata` here, using the same two small hunks #2305 has. Then adoption and session start use one resolver. That's a strict improvement for `--separate-git-dir` and bare-repo worktrees not named `.git`/`.bare` (like `storage`); split layouts fail before and after. #2305 drops those hunks when it's rebased. The reviewer offered this route.
- **Small items:** a Debug log in `bestEffortAdoptWorktreeID` (4), drop the doubled error wrapping (6), and resolve the source ID once and pass it down (7).
- **Tests:** add two regression tests and confirm they fail on the current head first:
  - import's session state and its checkpoints land in the same repo with an exported `GIT_DIR`, in both the split and redirect cases;
  - a session can start in a bare repo's linked worktree that adoption accepts.

  Delete the tests that pin the old claims: `TestStateStoreForWorktreeIgnoresRepositoryOverrides` and the explicit-root row in the subprocess-count test.
- **Leave 3 for later:** reply to the reviewer that it's already on `main`.
- **Afterwards:** `mise run check`, then I show you the rewritten PR description and the reply to the reviewer before anything is posted.

**Option B: shrink the PR**
Revert `state.go` and `session_adopt.go` to `main`. Keep the store/lock test, the comment fix, and the ledger text, and add the import regression test. All of the migration moves to #2305. This is the lowest risk, but #2285 would no longer change any production code, and #2305 gets bigger.

**Proposed review lessons**, for your approval, exact text:
- `cli.md`, sharpening the existing lesson: "When replacing a git subprocess with a filesystem parser, check that it still works in bare repos and still respects exported `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE`; git handles cases a parser misses. This includes functions that take an 'explicit' root: check where callers get it, since a root found through `paths.WorktreeRoot` already honors those variables."
- `General.md`, new: "When two code paths must agree on a location or ID (state and its lock, a list and its throttle, adoption and hooks), move them to a new resolver together or leave both on the old one; moving one side splits them silently."

# Blast Radius

Find what a change breaks somewhere else, before it ships.

Companion to `research-codebase` and `what-happened`. `research-codebase` tells
you what the code does. `what-happened` recovers why it is shaped that way.
Blast radius tells you what it breaks somewhere else.

Listing the callers is not the job. You can grep those in a second. The job is the breakage grep
won't show you.

## Use When

- The user asks for the blast radius of a change, or what it could break.
- You are reviewing a small diff you don't trust yet.
- A change touches a shared path, a wire format, or a dependency you don't own.

## Don't Trust Your Own Writeup

A blast-radius writeup that sounds right is worthless. It reads as convincing whether or not it's
true, and that is the trap. Don't hand back the writeup. Find the one or two facts the whole thing
depends on and prove them by running code. Words are where you start, not what you ship.

### How Sure Are You

For each fact the change's safety depends on, get it as far down this list as is cheap, and say
where it stopped.

1. You said so. Worthless on its own.
2. You pointed at the line. A real `file:line`, or the library's own source.
3. You showed the bad case can't happen. You walked the failure step by step and it doesn't reach.
4. You ran it. A script or test that calls the real code and fails loud if you're wrong.
5. You reproduced it in the running app.

Any safety fact you can't get to step 4, say so out loud. Don't write it up as settled. Step 4 is
usually one small script that imports the same library the app ships and calls the exact function
you're worried about.

## Do

1. **Read the change.** The diff, the symbols it adds, changes, and deletes, and what it now does
   differently, including the part the diff doesn't spell out. Pull the surrounding history with
   `git log -p $(git merge-base main HEAD)..HEAD` and `gh pr view` when a PR exists.
1b. **Sweep the mechanical radius with the graph when installed** (`entire graph version`
   succeeds). One call per changed symbol replaces the caller grep and adds what grep misses
   structurally — type consumers, data flows, co-change files:
   `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text`. For a branch-wide change list,
   `entire graph diff --base <base> --head HEAD --json`. Graph output is evidence, not an
   oracle — it can miss callers (dynamic dispatch, interfaces), so it bounds step 3, never
   replaces it.
2. **Find the one fact it's safe because of.** Most changes that look scary are safe because of a
   single fact, like "this call only drops already-dead cache entries and does nothing else". Find
   that fact. If it holds, most of the scary cases die at once. Spend your time here, not on a long
   list of maybes.
3. **Look where grep stops.** Read the source of the library you call, and check its pinned version
   and any local patch. Work out when things run: microtasks, unmount and teardown, framework
   scheduling differences. Follow what a symbol search misses: the JSON an API returns, a DB column,
   a wire format, another language reading the same bytes, a feature flag, code three hops downstream.
4. **Audit semantic callers of shared primitives.** When a lock, retry, context, subprocess, or
   environment helper changes, compare callers with a deadline, cancellation without a deadline,
   and neither. Trace blocking, fairness, error identity, cleanup, inherited environment, and the
   outermost workflow result. Symbol callers are not enough when the changed contract is scheduling
   or process behavior.
5. **Be honest about each risk.** Give it a real chance of happening and a real cost if it does.
   Keep the risks you confirmed; list the ones you checked and cleared separately. Cite a real
   `file:line`. A search that finds nothing is still an answer. Never make up a caller or an API.
6. **Prove the one fact.** Write a script or test that runs the real code, run it, and paste what
   happened. If you can't prove it cheaply, mark it unproven. Don't round up.
7. **For a big or wide change, run it as an `arena`.** Ask several models the same question and merge
   the answers. Different models catch different real bugs.

## Output

- **What it does.** What changed, including the part that isn't obvious.
- **The one fact it's safe because of.** State it, say which step you got it to, and show the proof.
  If you couldn't prove it, write unproven.
- **Risks.** Only the real ones. Each names how it breaks, the `file:line`, how likely and how bad,
  and how to check. Paste the proof for the ones that matter.
- **Cleared.** What you checked and why it's fine.
- **Before you merge.** The cheapest test or repro that catches the real bug, including the script
  you wrote.

Write it through `unslop`, cite real code, and strip anything private before it goes anywhere public.

## Stop When

The one safety fact is either proven at step 4 or explicitly marked unproven. A writeup that
asserts safety without naming which step its central fact reached means this failed.

Fixing all 8 touches three production files and about six test files. What users would see changes in one place that matters: every agent's session start. Everything else is confined to `entire import`, `entire session adopt`, and error and log text. The fact the hook change's safety depends on is proven by running real git repos.

**What "fix all 8" changes**

| Fix | File | Who sees it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1, 5, 6, 8: store back on `CommonDirForWorktree` | `session/state.go` | `entire import` and the import step in `entire setup` only. It's the only production caller ([agentimport.go:389](cmd/entire/cli/agentimport/agentimport.go:389)). This restores `main`'s behavior. |
| 2: hooks get the ID from the canonical resolver | `strategy/manual_commit_session.go:452,652` | **Every new session start for every agent**: `handleLifecycleTurnStart` → `InitializeSession`, plus `ensureSessionInitialized` ([manual_commit_git.go:186](cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_git.go:186)) |
| 3: strip `GIT_DIR` and related variables on adoption's source query | `session_adopt.go:488` | `entire session adopt`, and only when repo variables are exported |
| 4, 7: Debug log, look the source ID up once | `session_adopt.go` | Internal. `selectAdoptSourceSession` gets a new parameter, which ripples to `runAdopt` and about 5 test call sites |

Tests: delete `TestStateStoreForWorktreeIgnoresRepositoryOverrides` and the explicit-root row of the subprocess-count test, update the signature call sites, and add the regression tests. The PR description also needs a rewrite.

**The one fact it's safe because of**

*In every layout where session start works today, the new resolver returns the same `WorktreeID` the hooks already record.* If that holds, existing session state, `entire session list --json` (`worktree_id`, [sessions.go:587](cmd/entire/cli/sessions.go:587)), and adoption matching all stay the same.

I proved it by running a test that calls both real functions on real git repos, through a Go overlay so no repo files changed ([probe](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-muskanpaliwal-Work-open-source-entire-cli-refactor-session-metadata-resolution/700e8b16-5ef9-42d0-a9f6-5f00985b07be/scratchpad/blast/worktree_id_parity_test.go)):

```text
linked worktree                        "wt"      "wt"      same
linked worktree, duplicate basename    "wt1"     "wt1"     same
linked worktree, relative paths        "rel"     "rel"     same
linked worktree moved without repair   "tomove"  "tomove"  same

repo under a path with .git/worktrees/ "x/proj/.git/worktrees/oddwt"  "oddwt"  DIFFERENT
```

The fact holds for all 10 normal layouts. In the one that differs, the old parser is the one that's wrong: it cuts at the first `.git/worktrees/` in the path ([worktree.go:64](cmd/entire/cli/paths/worktree.go:64)).

**Real risks**

1. **Two layouts start running code they never ran before.** That's `--separate-git-dir` and bare repos not named `.git`/`.bare`. Session start used to fail there, so condensation, commit hooks and checkpointing have never run in those layouts. Likely to matter only for the few people who use them, and the cost is new hook errors. It's partly offset because the store, lock and checkpoint paths use the git subprocess, which handles these layouts. **Not proven.** The cheapest check is a test that starts a session and commits in each of the two layouts.
2. **One contrived path gets a new ID.** If a repo lives under a directory whose path contains `.git/worktrees/`, sessions recorded before the change keep the broken ID and new ones get the correct one. Adoption compares the two without falling back to the path ([session_adopt.go:567](cmd/entire/cli/session_adopt.go:567)), so old sessions would stop being adoption candidates there. Very unlikely and low cost.
3. **The later PRs interact with these fixes.**
   - #2305 contains the same two hook hunks. That's fine if they're identical, but its rebase has to take this version.
   - #2320 switches `NewStateStoreForWorktree` back to the env-blind resolver, which would bring finding 1 back. My note on #2305 flags the env decision but doesn't name #2320's store change.
4. **Fix 3 changes adoption when repo variables are exported.** I proved the bug it fixes: with `GIT_DIR=A` exported, `git -C B rev-parse --git-common-dir` returned A's `.git`, so today an exported `GIT_DIR` silently replaces the path the user passed. After the fix, adoption reads the path's own repo. Anyone relying on the old behavior would see a different session list, which seems unlikely to matter.

- Fix 1 only restores `main`'s code path, and its one production caller is import.
- `WorktreeID` isn't stored in checkpoint metadata. Its only JSON homes are session state and `session list --json`, and both stay the same in every normal layout.
- `status.go:951` reads `.git` from the worktree, but only for a branch label and it tolerates failure. It isn't on the hook path.
- Fixes 4 to 8 change no behavior outside adoption internals, error text and one debug log. The only test asserting the doubled error text is in the checkpoint package, which these fixes don't touch.

The merged part 2 (#2254) has the same pattern. [checkpoint/repository_metadata.go:29](cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/repository_metadata.go:29) takes the worktree root from the opened repo, then resolves it with the env-blind resolver; that feeds the redaction cache and the push queue. I haven't run this one; I'm going by the code. If I'm right, those fail in split layouts, and in a redirect they point at the local `.git`. Worth its own issue rather than adding to this PR.

**Before you merge**
- Make the parity probe a permanent test in `strategy`, written before the hook change.
- Add a test that a session starts and a commit condenses in the `--separate-git-dir` and bare `storage` layouts. That covers risk 1, the one thing I couldn't prove.
- Add the import regression test (state and checkpoints land in the same repo under an exported `GIT_DIR`), and confirm it fails on the current head first.
- Add one line to the #2305 note saying #2320's store change has to stay env-aware.

I stopped before any production edits, because two of the approved fixes turned out wrong or no longer enough. The only local change is a merge of `upstream/main` into the branch. It wasn't pushed, and I resolved one compile break in it.

**Finding 1 isn't a regression, and the approved fix would cause the bug the reviewer describes.**
- `entire import` opens its repository through `gitrepo.OpenPath`. That already uses the env-blind `ResolveWorktreeMetadata` on `main`, so checkpoints ignore `GIT_DIR` too.
- In the redirect case, the current PR's store agrees with the checkpoints. Going back to `CommonDirForWorktree` would send the state to repo B and the checkpoints to repo A.
- In the split case, import fails loudly at `openRepository` before it writes any state, and it did on `main` too. So imported sessions never silently go missing.
- Revised fix: keep the store as it is, but fix 5 (drop the unused `ctx`), 6 (a clearer error that doesn't repeat the root) and 8 (restore `filepath.Abs`). Add a guard test that import's state and checkpoints land in the same repo under an exported `GIT_DIR`. It passes today, and I'll confirm it fails if the reviewer's suggested revert is applied.

**Finding 2 grew after the merge.**
- `main` added worktree-incarnation markers and cross-worktree linking. They look up worktree IDs with `paths.GetWorktreeID` in about 10 hook call sites, in `worktree_home.go`, `worktree_work.go`, `turn_worktree.go` and `manual_commit_session.go`.
- Moving only the 2 calls I had scoped would leave hooks recording IDs one way and checking them another.
- Revised fix: put adoption's source and target IDs back on `GetWorktreeID` behind one helper, which also covers fixes 4 and 7. That matches every hook path exactly and opens no new layouts.
- The cost: adoption in a bare repo named `storage` goes back to failing, and its test goes away. The parity and new-layout tests belong with whichever PR moves all 10 hook sites. #2305 predates those sites, so it needs reworking anyway.
- The alternative is to move all 10 sites here. Same IDs in every normal layout (the parity run proved that), but two new layouts open across the brand-new linking code, and the PR grows a lot.

**Fix 3 is unchanged, with one correction.** `stateStoreForWorktree` also resolves the target (`"."`), so only the source query gets `EnvWithoutRepoOverrides`. The target keeps honoring `GIT_DIR` so it matches the hooks' store. I'll add a test that fails first.

input.content:
Part 3 of #2190's [agreed split](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2190#issuecomment-5499945525), following the merged canonical resolver in #2241 and checkpoint migration in #2254.

The explicit-root session store still ran a Git subprocess to find its common directory, while the repository it serves is opened through `gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata`. This PR moves the store to that resolver and fixes how `entire session adopt` resolves its source repository and worktree IDs.

## Session-store construction

Previously, constructing a session store for a known worktree root ran `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, even though the root was already known.

`NewStateStoreForWorktree` now resolves `WorktreeMetadata.CommonDir` directly. Known-root construction therefore starts no Git subprocesses and checks the current metadata on every call. For example, if `commondir` is changed to point at a missing directory after a successful construction, the next construction fails. Repairing the metadata makes construction succeed again and preserves access to the saved session.

Its only production caller is `entire import`, which opens its repository with `strategy.OpenRepository`. That opener reads the worktree's own `.git` through the same resolver, so session state and checkpoints now come from one repository. This matters when `GIT_DIR` is exported:

- If the worktree has its own `.git` and `GIT_DIR` names another repository, import writes checkpoints to the worktree's repository. On `main`, the Git subprocess followed `GIT_DIR`, so the imported session state went to the other repository, where `entire session list` could not pair it with its checkpoints.
- If `GIT_DIR` and `GIT_WORK_TREE` are both exported and the work tree has no `.git`, import stops at `strategy.OpenRepository`, on `main` and on this branch, before any state is written.

`NewStateStoreForWorktree` also drops its unused context parameter, and its error now names worktree metadata instead of calling every failure a common-directory problem. The test-isolation guard keeps resolving relative paths before it compares against the temp root.

`NewStateStore`, the CWD constructor, intentionally stays on `gitdir.CommonDir`. The strategy's per-session state lock resolves through that same function, and the store and its lock must agree on one common directory. If the store moved to the canonical resolver alone, an exported `GIT_DIR` would place state files in the worktree's own `.git` while the lock went to the repository `GIT_DIR` names. Two writers of one state file would then hold different locks. Keeping both on one resolver also keeps split `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` setups working for session state. The CWD store moves to the canonical resolver together with the lock.

The common directory still feeds the existing rooted store. Linked worktrees share session files, and empty-root rejection, no-follow I/O, atomic writes, and locking remain in place.

## Adoption

Adoption keeps `paths.GetWorktreeID` for source and target worktree IDs. Session start, the worktree-home checks, and cross-worktree linking all derive IDs with it, so an adopted session carries the ID those hooks reproduce. Moving adoption alone to the canonical resolver would accept worktrees that session start rejects, such as a linked worktree of a bare repository named `storage`, and save sessions whose ID the hooks never match. These lookups move together in the strategy migration.

The source worktree ID is now resolved once per adoption and passed down instead of being read again at each step. When it cannot be derived, adoption still matches sessions by their recorded path, and the reason is logged at debug level.

The source query now drops inherited repository selectors. An exported `GIT_DIR` selects Git's repository even under `git -C`, so `entire session adopt --from <path>` read the current repository's sessions instead of those at the path the user named. The target query still inherits them, so it resolves the same store the hooks use. The combined Git query in `stateStoreForWorktree` stays because it validates an arbitrary user-supplied repository; a directory that merely contains an empty `.git` folder must still be rejected. Source-retirement rollback remains unchanged.

## Why the legacy APIs and cache remain

`session.GetGitCommonDir`, the cache-clearing API, and `gitdir`'s common-directory resolver and cache still serve the CWD session store, the session lock, the session sweep, the review manifest, strategy, and other consumers outside this slice. Removing them now would require migrating those callers too. Their deletion waits until those callers have migrated and been verified.

The sweep stays on `session.GetGitCommonDir` on purpose. It finds stuck sessions through the CWD store, so its throttle marker has to come from the same resolver. Moving the sweep alone to the canonical resolver would break split `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` layouts: the work tree has no `.git`, so the sweep would find stuck sessions and then skip spawning on every session start. The sweep moves together with the CWD store.

This PR changes two production files and their tests, plus the one import call site and a comment-only fix in `gitdir/gitdir.go` that drops a stale list of callers. The ownership guard remains active, and its ledger reasons now name the callers that still use the legacy resolvers. Rooted-handle lifetime and the strategy and session-lock migration stay with their existing owners.

## For the strategy migration

A probe across main, linked, duplicate-basename, relative-path, moved, symlinked, `.bare`, submodule, and submodule-worktree layouts found the same worktree IDs from `paths.GetWorktreeID` and `gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata`. They differ in three layouts: `--separate-git-dir` main worktrees and bare repositories with other names, where the legacy parser fails, and a repository whose path contains `.git/worktrees/`, where the legacy parser cuts at the first match.

## Verification

VERIFICATION_PLACEHOLDER

- Written before the fixes and failing on the previous revision:
  - `TestSessionAdopt_SourcePathWinsOverExportedGitDir` failed with `session ... was not found in <source>`.
  - `TestBuildAdoptedStateRejectsWorktreesSessionStartRejects` failed because adoption succeeded where session start cannot derive an ID.
  - `TestTestIsolationGuardResolvesRelativeCommonDir` failed with the test-isolation error.
- `TestRun_SessionStateFollowsCheckpointRepositoryUnderExportedGitDir` passes on this branch and fails when the store goes back to the Git subprocess: the state lands in the `GIT_DIR` repository while checkpoints stay in the worktree's.

Focused tests cover linked-worktree save/load/clear, invalid roots, explicit-root metadata damage and repair, inherited Git variables on explicit roots, adoption validation, and the source-path fallback when the source worktree ID cannot be derived. `TestSessionStateAndLockHonorExportedGitDir` pins that the CWD store and its lock land in the same common directory when `GIT_DIR` points at another repository and in a split `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` layout. Existing tests exercise rooted storage, symlink refusal, and adoption rollback.

Real Git Trace2 events show constructor subprocess counts:

| Construction path | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CWD | 1 common-directory query | 1 common-directory query (unchanged) |
| Explicit root | 1 | 0 |

The Trace2 test includes a positive control that launches Git and checks that an additional event is recorded. These measurements cover store construction, not total hook latency.
